'''Benjamin Fain''' ({{langx|ru|Вениамин Моисеевич Файн}}, {{langx|he|בנימין פיין}}; February 17, 1930 – April 15, 2013) was an Israeli physicist, professor-emeritus, and former [[refusenik]].

==Biography==

Fain was born to a Jewish family in [[Kyiv]]. His father was a mathematician. He instilled in the child a love for science as well as a strong national sentiment.<ref>"Creation Ex Nihilo", part 2 of Russian version</ref>

Benjamin Fain was named after his grandfather, who was murdered in the [[Proskurov pogrom]]. During the [[Second World War]] the family was evacuated and changed location several times. After the end of the war the family stayed in [[Dushanbe]], where Fain graduated from school. He became a student in the [[Moscow Power Engineering Institute|Moscow Institute of Energetics]]. During his first year in [[Moscow]] he visited [[synagogue]] and attempted to learn the [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]] and [[Yiddish language|Yiddish]] languages. Fain was strongly impressed by the historical visit of the first Israeli ambassador to [[USSR]], [[Golda Meir]]. Fain managed to transfer in 1950 to the Faculty of [[physics]] in [[N. I. Lobachevsky State University of Nizhny Novgorod|Gorky University]]. He graduated there [[summa cum laude]]. His instructor was future [[Nobel Prize]] winner [[Vitaly Ginzburg]].

==Academic career==
Fain successfully started his scientific career, and already in 1965 became a professor in his [[alma mater]]. He wrote several scientific books translated into English and German.<ref>{{cite book|title=Fain: Quantum Electronics|id={{ASIN|0262060302|country=uk}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B0000EG6EC|title=Quantenelektronik: Physik der Maser und Laser|publisher=Teubner|year=1969}}</ref><ref>[http://www.allbookstores.com/Benjamin-Fain/author Books by Benjamin Fain], [https://openlibrary.org/a/OL972350A Books by B. Fain]</ref> In 1966 he moved to Moscow and started successful work in the [[Institute of Solid State Physics (Russia)|Institute of Solid State Physics]] in [[Chernogolovka]]. 
[[File:Seminar of scientists refuseniks.jpg|thumb|250px|Fain on the right side, [[Andrei Sakharov]] — on the left side. Unofficial seminar of scientists-[[refusenik]]s, April 1977]]
Starting from 1972 Fain gradually started to participate in a [[Zionism|Zionist]] movement. He took part in [[refusenik]] scientific seminar, and also in [[Samizdat]].<ref>[http://www.jewish-heritage.org/jr1a5r.htm Матвей Членов. "ЕВРЕЙСКИЙ САМИЗДАТ В СОВЕТСКОМ СОЮЗЕ", 1970-Е — 1980-Е ГОДЫ] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081205095729/http://www.jewish-heritage.org/jr1a5r.htm |date=December 5, 2008 }}: В 1975 году, за год до симпозиума, по инициативе В.Файна и Престина начинает издаваться журнал "Тарбут"</ref> He applied for exit visa to Israel in 1974 and became a [[refusenik]]. He also became unemployed after dismissal from his work on political grounds.

==Sociological research of Soviet Jewry==
In 1976 Fain initiated a sociological research on [[History of the Jews in the Soviet Union|Soviet Jewry]]. An attempt to organize an international symposium on the subject was foiled by the [[KGB]],<ref>[http://www.lechaim.ru/ARHIV/102/begun.htm "Сегодня рождается из вчера." Иосиф Бегун]. К истории еврейской общины в Москве</ref> which closely watched all his steps from then on. At the same period Fain gradually started practicing [[Judaism]]. After several arrests, searches, interrogations and a hunger strike Fain finally arrived in Israel in 1977.

Fain published his study on [[Jewish identity]] of [[Soviet Jews]] with the American sociologist [[Mervin Verbit]]. Fain and Verbit published their findings in 1984 through the [[Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs]].<ref>Fain, B., & Verbit, M. F. (1984). Jewishness in the Soviet Union: Report of an Empirical Survey. Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs.</ref>

==In Israel==
He continued to struggle to improve the life of Soviet Jews and also continued his scientific work in [[Tel Aviv University]] in the fields of [[quantum electronics]], [[laser]]s and [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter]].<ref>[http://www.tau.ac.il/chemistry/fain/ Benjamin Fain, Professor Emeritus]</ref>

Starting from 1998 his field of interest moved to the [[philosophy of science]] and Judaism and the interrelation between them. After retirement Fain wrote his first philosophic book in Hebrew: "Creation Ex Nihilo", where he analyzes the relationship between [[religion]] and [[science]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.allbookstores.com/Creation-Nihilo-Thoughts-Science-Divine/9789652293992|title=Creation Ex Nihilo : Thoughts on Science, Divine Providence, Free Will, and Faith in the Perspective of My Own Experiences|date=20 July 2007}}</ref> It was published in Hebrew as well as in English and Russian translations. The Russian version of the book also has an autobiographic part to it.

In 2008 Fain completed another book in Hebrew: "Law and Providence".<ref>{{langx|he|חוק והשגחה. הוצאת מכון הספרים הר ברכה תשס"ט}}</ref> It was published in 2011 in English by [[Urim Publications]]. In January 2011 Fain's third book {{langx|he|«דלות הכפירה» («Dalut Ha'kfira» («The Poverty of Secularism»)}} was published by {{langx|he|[[:he:מוסד הרב קוק|Mosad Ha'rav Kook]]}}.

==Children==
Fain is the father of two sons and one daughter.
